items.t: Hon Hai stock: Foxconn lifts outlook after record Q3 profit
sum: Foxconn reported record third-quarter results on Thursday, November 12, as demand for AI servers lifted growth across the business. The company also raised its full-year outlook for all four major product segments.

According to the Hon Hai Technology Group, third-quarter revenue reached NT$3.02 trillion, up 46 percent from a year earlier. Operating profit rose 64 percent to NT$115.4 billion, while net profit attributable to owners of the parent company increased 34 percent to NT$77.5 billion.

Cloud and networking products, supported by AI server demand, were the main growth engine. Foxconn said the business is improving its product mix and customer base as AI infrastructure investment expands.
Earnings per share reached NT$5.51 for the July-to-September quarter. For the first nine months, revenue rose 39 percent to NT$7.66 trillion and net profit increased 30 percent to NT$187.4 billion.

Foxconn expects strong fourth-quarter growth both sequentially and year over year. It raised its full-year outlook for smart consumer electronics, cloud and networking, computing, and components and other products. Management also expressed confidence in continued growth in 2027.
The outlook remains exposed to tight supplies of chips, memory and other components. Foxconn expects new capacity to ease bottlenecks gradually, but demand may continue to exceed supply next year.

Hon Hai stock: Record profit strengthens AI growth outlook
sum: Hon Hai Technology Group, better known as Foxconn, reported record third-quarter results on Thursday, November 12, as demand for AI servers lifted revenue and profitability. In its financial release, the company said all four major product segments had a stronger outlook for the full year.
Hon Hai stock traded at 12.80 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 09:35 CET on Friday, November 13. The quote reflects the company’s U.S. dollar-denominated security traded in euros on that venue.

Foxconn generated revenue of NT$3.02 trillion in the July-to-September quarter, up 46 percent from the same period a year earlier and 19 percent from the second quarter. Gross profit rose 39 percent to NT$181.5 billion, operating profit increased 64 percent to NT$115.4 billion, and net profit attributable to owners of the parent company climbed 34 percent to NT$77.5 billion.

Earnings per share reached NT$5.51, compared with NT$4.15 a year earlier and NT$4.27 in the second quarter. The company reported a gross margin of 6.02 percent, an operating margin of 3.83 percent and a net margin of 2.57 percent. For the first nine months, revenue increased 39 percent to NT$7.66 trillion and net profit rose 30 percent to NT$187.4 billion.

Cloud and networking products, including AI servers, were the main source of the record revenue. Foxconn said the segment exceeded its most optimistic initial expectations, while Chairman Young Liu described AI servers as the group’s most important growth engine. The division accounted for 54 percent of third-quarter revenue, up from 51 percent in the second quarter.

Foxconn expects strong sequential and year-over-year growth in the fourth quarter. A new generation of AI server racks should support further growth in cloud and networking products, while the traditional peak season is expected to lift smart consumer electronics shipments. The company also cited higher average selling prices in consumer electronics.

Management raised its outlook across all four major product segments after operational performance exceeded earlier expectations. Computing products remain constrained by tight memory supplies and may decline slightly from the second quarter, although higher component prices are expected to support significant year-over-year growth.

Taiwan's Microelectronics Technology to Delist as Net Worth Turns Negative; Shares Lock at Limit-Down With Nearly 10,000 Sell Orders Queued
sum: Veteran satellite communications maker Microelectronics Technology (2314.TW) will be delisted on December 21 after its net worth turned negative. The stock gapped down at the open on November 11 and locked at the limit-down price of NT$6.66, with limit-down sell orders at one point approaching 10,000 lots, leaving investors unable to sell even if they wanted to.

According to the company's third-quarter consolidated financial report, its net worth has turned negative at NT$244 million (approximately $7.4 million), with a debt ratio of 109% and a current ratio of 65%. Its accountants issued an audit report citing "material uncertainty about the company's ability to continue as a going concern," putting it out of compliance with relevant provisions of the Taiwan Stock Exchange's operating rules. After Microelectronics Technology held a material information briefing on November 10, the Taiwan Stock Exchange announced that evening that the company's shares would be delisted effective December 21.

On the earnings front, Microelectronics Technology posted a net loss of NT$463 million (approximately $14.1 million) for the first three quarters of this year, a loss per share of NT$4.33. The third quarter alone saw a net loss per share of NT$2.61 and a quarterly loss of about NT$284 million (approximately $8.6 million), exceeding the cumulative loss of the first half. Revenue momentum was similarly weak, with October revenue of just NT$42.07 million (approximately $1.3 million), down 87.52% from a year earlier.

Microelectronics Technology was once a flagship of Taiwan's satellite communications industry, drawing global attention for its satellite communications technology during the Gulf War. Its share price once climbed to NT$242 in 1991, and it once received an NT$1.8 billion (approximately $54.8 million) investment from Hon Hai Group. In recent years, however, its operations have deteriorated. Market observers attribute the decline to several factors, including the slower-than-expected development of 5G open radio access networks (O-RAN), the failure of its low-earth-orbit (LEO) satellite business to contribute profits in time, and the severe blow dealt to its subsidiaries by the U.S.-China trade war.

Hon Hai stock: Record October sales sharpen AI growth focus
sum: Hon Hai Precision Industry, better known as Foxconn, posted record consolidated revenue for October as demand for AI products, consumer electronics and computing equipment remained strong. The figures were reported in the company's unaudited monthly revenue release and covered the month ended October 31.

The Economic Times reported that October revenue reached NT$1.305 trillion, an increase of 45.73 percent from October 2025. Revenue also rose 12.66 percent from September, making October the company's highest-revenue month on record.

Cloud and networking products, the segment most closely linked to AI infrastructure, showed strong year-on-year growth as customers pulled forward AI-related orders. The segment declined slightly from September, however, with Foxconn citing changes in the consignment model, tight supply conditions and the initial ramp-up of new models.

All four major product categories grew year on year. Smart consumer electronics benefited from higher shipment prices and stronger customer demand, while computing products gained from higher shipment prices and early shipments of new products. Components and other products also recorded stronger demand.

Revenue for January through October reached NT$8.98 trillion, up 40.40 percent from the same period a year earlier. In US dollar terms, the ten-month increase was 38.4 percent, although the reported figures had not been reviewed or audited by a certified public accountant.

Foxconn said AI-related operations should continue growing in the fourth quarter. The company expects the traditional second-half peak season for information and communications technology products to support overall performance in line with current market expectations. It also cautioned that the global political and economic environment remains volatile.

The next major operating test comes with Foxconn's third-quarter results conference on November 12. The company's November monthly revenue report is expected on December 5, giving investors a further indication of whether AI-related demand and new-model production ramps are sustaining the recent sales momentum.

Stock Futures Tick Up as Traders Await Inflation Data and AI Earnings
sum: Stock futures demonstrated a slight uptick on Sunday evening as traders remained focused on the potential recovery of technology shares. Anticipation was building for the upcoming inflation data and earnings reports from major artificial intelligence companies scheduled for the week ahead. Specifically, S&P 500 futures recorded a gain of 0.1%, while the Nasdaq 100 futures increased by 0.3%. Additionally, futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average saw an increase of 101 points, equivalent to 0.2%.

Over in Asia, markets exhibited mostly positive performance on Monday, with Taiwanese equities leading the charge. The Taiwan Weighted Index surged nearly 5%, buoyed by a significant rebound in key stocks such as TSMC and Hon Hai Precision Industry, widely recognized as Foxconn. The Nikkei 225 in Japan climbed by 3.25%, while the Topix index increased by 3.44%, largely supported by gains in financial and consumer cyclical stocks. South Korea’s Kospi index rose by 1.15%, overcoming an initial decline, whereas the small-cap Kosdaq index dipped by 0.23%. Major tech companies Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix experienced gains of 2.49% and 2.03%, respectively. In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng Index rose 1.03%, while the CSI 300 index in mainland China was up by 0.3%.

Investors in Asia were also focused on October inflation data from China, which revealed the producer price index reaching its highest point in over four years at 5.7%. In contrast, consumer inflation came in slower than anticipated at 0.7%. Meanwhile, Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 faced a decline of 0.51%.

The preceding Friday had witnessed a partial rebound from Thursday’s significant selloff driven by AI-related concerns, as chip stocks experienced renewed buying interest. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite rose by 1.09% to 24,579.42, and the broad-market S&P 500 increased by 0.31% to 7,376.86. Conversely, the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average fell by 237.33 points, or 0.46%, ending at 51,285.73. Broader investor sentiment remained cautious amidst stronger-than-expected jobs data, and concerns persisted following robust midterm election results for Democrats.

sum: Foxconn reported record monthly revenue for October on November 5, giving investors a fresh indication of demand across its electronics manufacturing business. Focus Taiwan said Hon Hai Precision Industry generated NT$1.3 trillion in consolidated revenue, up 45.73 percent from a year earlier and 12.66 percent from September.

The October performance extended a strong run for the company. Revenue for the first ten months of 2026 reached a record NT$8.98 trillion, an increase of 40.40 percent from the same period a year earlier. The figures were unaudited and were submitted to the Taiwan Stock Exchange.

Cloud and networking products remained supported by demand for artificial intelligence applications, although the segment slipped slightly from September because of changes in the consignment model, supply constraints and the initial ramp-up of new products. Foxconn said it expects its AI-related business to keep growing in the fourth quarter.

A separate report published by Yahoo Finance on November 4 described Chairman Young Liu's ambition to lift Foxconn's AI-server market share from about 40 percent to as much as 50 percent within the next two years. The company expects servers, racks and related infrastructure to contribute between 60 percent and 65 percent of revenue within three to five years, excluding edge AI devices.

Capacity is fully booked for at least 18 months, according to the report. Foxconn also plans to expand its US manufacturing activities and currently allocates between 3 billion and 5 billion US dollars annually to AI-related activities. The expansion raises the growth opportunity while also increasing the importance of investment discipline and customer diversification.

Foxconn expects its overall performance to remain in line with market expectations and will present its third-quarter results at an investor conference call on November 12. The November revenue update is expected on December 5, providing another near-term indicator for AI infrastructure demand and the broader electronics cycle.

sum: Asian stocks suffered brutal sell-offs on Friday, with Taiwan and South Korea taking the biggest hits as investors turned cautious amid AI fears. The plunge came as Wall Street witnessed its worst session in 18 months, wiping out $2.5 trillion in investor wealth in one of the biggest single-day losses.
Asian stock markets witnessed a broad-based sell-off on Friday, with Taiwan and South Korea bearing the brunt of the losses as the rout in technology stocks spread across the region.

The sell-off saw Taiwan's weighted index plunge 8%, while South Korea's KOSPI dropped more than 7%. Japan's Nikkei 225 also declined over 3,000 points or 5.95%. The losses extended to Singapore, where the Straits Times index fell 2.20% to 5,180. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was also trading lower during early trading.

Technology stocks were among the worst hit, with semiconductor companies facing particularly heavy selling. South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix plunged more than 8%, while Samsung Electronics shed 7%. LG Innotek and LG Display also fell 10% and 7.7%, respectively, as investors dumped technology shares across the country.

Japanese technology stocks were not spared either. Semiconductor-related companies witnessed sharp declines, with chip-testing equipment maker Advantest plunging 12.2% and Tokyo Electron sliding 7.3%.
Memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings fell nearly 10%, while Renesas Electronics declined 7.5%.

Taiwan's semiconductor sector also came under intense pressure. Contract chipmaker TSMC slumped 9.6%, while electronics manufacturers Hon Hai Precision Industry, also known as Foxconn, and Foxconn Technology dropped 9.4% and 9.1%, respectively.

That wait-and-see atmosphere carried over to the Taiwan stock market, where the weighted index opened Thursday (Nov. 5) at 42,666.13 points, down 282.78 points. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing closed that day at NT$2,260, down NT$35, indicating that market concerns about the post-election policy direction had not dissipated with the announcement of the results.

Taiwan Stocks Plunge 1,612 Points in a Single Day; Guo Zherong Cites Nomura Report: Negative Cash Flow Misread, Not a Bearish Signal
sum: Taiwan's Weighted Index opened lower and fell further on the 3rd, touching an intraday low of 43,191.58 before closing down 1,612.60 points, or 3.59%, at 43,307.54 — decisively breaking below the 44,000-point threshold — with single-day turnover of NT$928.058 billion (approximately $28.3 billion). Measured over the past month, the benchmark has now tumbled roughly 6,000 points, and concerns over whether a bear market has officially arrived are heating up rapidly. Moore Investment Advisory Chief Investment Officer Guo Zherong stepped forward at this juncture, citing the latest Nomura Securities report to argue that the selloff stems from excessive market sentiment rather than a deterioration in corporate fundamentals. He stressed that "the market will eventually give fundamentals their due."

Guo Zherong analyzed that the market has been continuously magnifying political uncertainty ahead of the U.S. election as well as the disruption to oil prices and market sentiment from shifting U.S.-Iran tensions. These headline factors have become reasons for investors to sell holdings, but they should not be equated directly with a deteriorating corporate profit outlook. He believes that once panic gradually subsides, capital will ultimately re-examine corporate earnings and industry trends, giving the market a chance to return to fundamentals. He therefore maintained his medium- to long-term view that the Taiwan Weighted Index will challenge 50,000 by year-end and reach 100,000 over the next three years.

The Nomura Securities report cited by Guo Zherong centers on clarifying a misunderstanding about the AI industry. The report notes that investors have directly interpreted cloud giants' "negative free cash flow" as "AI is unprofitable and earnings are declining," when in fact they are conflating two concepts: profit and cash flow. Cloud providers are currently in the early stage of heavy investment in AI infrastructure, aggressively purchasing GPUs and developing their own TPU chips; it is the massive capital expenditure that has temporarily turned cash flow negative. Yet the three major cloud providers posted year-on-year revenue growth of 56% over the same period, showing that real demand for AI computing power remains strong.

Taiwan's Delta Electronics Stock Halves From Peak; Market Cap Overtaken by Hon Hai, Slips to No. 4
sum: The Taiwan stock market fell sharply intraday on November 3, and shares of AI power supply leader Delta Electronics (2308.TW) hit new lows in tandem, ending the session down NT$85, or 6.27%, at NT$1,270 — an eight-month low. Compared with the intraday peak of NT$2,585 set in late May, the stock has effectively halved. Market capitalization rankings were reshuffled accordingly, with Delta overtaken by Hon Hai (2317.TW) and knocked out of the top three listed companies to fourth place.

According to Taiwan Stock Exchange market capitalization statistics for listed companies, Delta's latest market value is NT$3.2988 trillion (approximately $100.6 billion), while Hon Hai climbed to third place at NT$3.4555 trillion (approximately $105.4 billion). Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (2330.TW) remains the market cap leader at NT$59.5147 trillion (approximately $1.8 trillion), with MediaTek (2454.TW) second at NT$5.8981 trillion (approximately $179.9 billion); ASE Technology Holding (3711.TW) ranks fifth at NT$3.0131 trillion (approximately $91.9 billion). The top five market cap companies are all electronics heavyweights.

In fact, the two companies' market values had already crossed at the November 2 close. That day, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing's market value was about NT$60.4224 trillion (approximately $1.8 trillion) and MediaTek's about NT$6.3717 trillion (approximately $194.3 billion), with Hon Hai at NT$3.533 trillion (approximately $107.7 billion) taking third place and Delta close behind at NT$3.5197 trillion (approximately $107.3 billion) — a gap of only about NT$13.3 billion (approximately $405.6 million). Delta touched its limit-down price of NT$1,335 intraday on October 30; although it rebounded NT$20 to close at NT$1,355 on November 2, Hon Hai rose 2.24% the same day, and Delta failed to hold its ranking. The stock weakened further on November 3; based on the intraday low of NT$1,310, its market value was about NT$3.4 trillion (approximately $103.7 billion), evaporating roughly another NT$116.9 billion (approximately $3.6 billion) from the prior trading day.

[HONG KONG] Taiwanese tech firms have completed a record US$14.5 billion of debt deals so far this year, as they race to secure financing to meet soaring demand for artificial intelligence capacity.

Hardware manufacturers such as chip component makers and server builders, vital parts of the global AI supply chain, have been driving the surge in borrowing as procurement and capital expenditure needs accelerate. The trend mirrors a global debt binge by tech companies as they build up AI infrastructure.

Taiwanese tech firms play a crucial role in the development of AI capacity, with Nvidia, Microsoft and OpenAI increasingly relying on them to fabricate their chips and build their servers. That’s helped boost shares of not only tech behemoths such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and Hon Hai Precision Industry, but also those of smaller AI players, turning the island’s stock market into the fifth largest in the world.

Of the total amount of financing, loans made up the biggest chunk, with US$6.2 billion in deals so far this year, while tech firms issued US$5.9 billion of convertible bonds and US$2.4 billion of corporate notes.

“AI has substantially scaled up the value and complexity of traditional server hardware,” said Randy Abrams, head of research at UBS Taiwan. Manufacturers need more working capital as they upgrade production lines and invest in new facilities in North America and South-east Asia to meet demand, he added.

Among the largest borrowings in the pipeline is Hon Hai’s up to US$1.5 billion convertible bond to help fund the procurement of materials from overseas. That follows a US$1.1 billion-equivalent loan the firm raised in February. Hon Hai, long known for its work assembling iPhones for Apple, expects AI hardware to be its key growth driver this year, as the business has surpassed smartphones as the biggest contributor to sales.

items.t: 2026: AI Servers to Be Extremely Expensive
sum: In 2026, it will be a crucial window period for the system-level upgrade of AI servers.

Correspondingly, there will be more effective power supply solutions, standard liquid cooling solutions, and higher requirements for PCBs and high-speed interconnections. This system-level upgrade will also make AI servers in 2026 "incredibly expensive."

Morgan Stanley predicts that for NVIDIA's platform alone, the demand for AI server cabinets will soar from approximately 28,000 units in 2025 to at least 60,000 units in 2026, more than doubling. Meanwhile, AMD's Helios server rack project (based on the MI400 series) has also made good progress, further intensifying the market's demand for advanced AI hardware.
Currently, NVIDIA's Blackwell platform, especially the GB200 chip, is the core driving force in the current AI server market.
In 2026, AI hardware will shift from the H00/H200 era to a new cycle driven by NVIDIA's GB200/300 (Blackwell platform) and the subsequent Vera Rubin (VR series) platform.

The power consumption of chips continues to break through the upper limit. From the 700W TDP (TDP: Thermal Design Power) of the H100, to 1000W of the B200, then to 1200W of the GB200, and finally to the Vera Rubin (VR200) platform that will debut in the second half of 2026, the maximum TDP of its GPU will soar to 2300W, and the VR200 NVL44 CPX at the end of 2026 will reach as high as 3700W.

As the GPU power consumption approaches 4kW, traditional air cooling solutions are completely ineffective, and liquid cooling has become the only viable option. NVIDIA has made liquid cooling a standard configuration on the GB200 platform and is jointly developing customized cold plate interfaces with major OEM manufacturers to ensure efficient heat transfer to the cooling circuit.

The chairmen of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and Hon Hai Precision Industry were there, surrounded by a sea of local manufacturing titans.
In a group photo to mark the event stood a man – tucked in the back row, wearing a dark shirt – who few would recognise: Chen Tao.

That unassuming presence belies his growing influence. The 53-year-old former soldier, who once served in China’s Taklamakan Desert, has become one of the country’s richest artificial intelligence (AI) billionaires, his fortune built on the world’s insatiable demand for the technology and a critical partnership with Nvidia.

Chen is the founder and chairman of Victory Giant Technology Huizhou, which manufactures printed circuit boards (PCBs), the intricate electronic backbone for the AI servers. As Nvidia’s GPUs became the engines of the AI revolution, Victory Giant, which is based in the city of Huizhou in China’s Guangdong province, to the north of Hong Kong, has emerged as one of its core suppliers.

The demand has sent Victory Giant stock soaring, making it this year’s top-performer on the MSCI Asia-Pacific Index with gains of more than 530 per cent. While its valuation is 32 times estimated earnings, that’s a fraction of the 100-plus multiples seen by other local chipmakers.

The surge gives Chen and his wife, Liu Chunlan, a combined net worth of US$9.1 billion as at the Nov 25 close, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, vaulting them above the likes of Pershing Square Capital Management founder Bill Ackman and Blackstone’s President Jon Gray. AI data center mostly booked: Hon Hai
sum: Manufacturing giant Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (鴻海精密) yesterday said that clients have already booked 70 to 80 percent of the computing power at its artificial intelligence (AI) data center in Kaohsiung.
Hon Hai in May announced a partnership with Nvidia Corp to build the data center in the city’s Asia New Bay Area (亞洲新灣區).

Hon Hai said it would purchase 10,000 GB300 chips based on Nvidia’s Blackwell Ultra architecture to provide up to 27MW of computing power in the center’s first phase of development, positioning it as a local AI inference hub.
Four clients have booked computing power at the data center, Hon Hai spokesman James Wu (巫俊毅) said on the sidelines of a news conference in Taipei, without naming the clients.
The center is to begin operations in the first half of next year, with a second phase of development being planned, Hon Hai said.

The company has intensified its efforts in AI development in the past few years to diversify its product portfolio. Last month, the company’s board of directors approved a NT$42 billion (US$1.345 billion) investment plan to purchase AI equipment for the data center.
Hon Hai plans to grow its AI deployment vertically and horizontally, Wu said.

items.t: Hon Hai reports record-high Q3 profit
sum: Manufacturing giant Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (鴻海精密) yesterday posted its best third-quarter profit in the company’s history, backed by strong demand for artificial intelligence (AI) servers.
Net profit expanded 17 percent annually to NT$57.67 billion (US$1.86 billion) from NT$44.36 billion, the company said.
On a quarterly basis, net profit soared 30 percent from NT$44.36 billion, it said.

Hon Hai, which is Apple Inc’s primary iPhone assembler and makes servers powered by Nvidia Corp’s AI accelerators, said earnings per share expanded to NT$4.15 from NT$3.55 a year earlier and NT$3.19 in the second quarter.

Gross margin improved to 6.35 percent, up from 6.19 percent a year earlier and 6.33 percent in the previous quarter, which the company attributed to better vertical integration of its products and a larger operational scale.

The growth momentum in AI servers is expected to extend into next year and the following two to three years, as the “major five” cloud service providers have raised their capital expenditure to about US$600 billion for next year, Hon Hai chairman Young Liu (劉揚偉) told investors yesterday.

“I am very optimistic about the development of the AI market next year. Our cooperation with clients and partners will be closer, and we expect to secure more orders by engaging in a wider range of AI projects,” Liu said. “Briefly, I am very positive about our outlook for 2026.”
